title: The Lahore Resolution and the idea of a separate state
detail: The Lahore Resolution was adopted in 1940, bringing the idea of a separate state for Muslims in the subcontinent to the center of politics. It was moved by A. K. Fazlul Huq, which made Bengal's political role especially significant.

title: The Bengal famine and social collapse
detail: The Bengal famine of 1943 killed millions. The failure of British administration deepened public anger and intensified political instability across the province.

title: The postwar political crisis
detail: After World War II, the end of British rule became more likely. But disagreements between the Congress Party and the Muslim League over the transfer of power grew sharper.

title: Elections and political polarization
detail: In the provincial elections, the Muslim League won overwhelming support in Bengal. The demand for a separate state became stronger, and political division became more visible.

title: Direct Action Day and communal violence
detail: Direct Action Day was followed by devastating communal violence in Calcutta and other parts of Bengal. The riots severely damaged Hindu-Muslim relations and made political compromise far more difficult.

title: The United Bengal proposal fails
detail: A proposal for an independent, united Bengal emerged under leaders such as Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy and Sarat Chandra Bose. It failed amid political mistrust and opposition from central leadership.

title: The partition plan is announced
detail: Lord Mountbatten announced the plan for partition, setting India on the final path toward division. Bengal and Punjab, both demographically mixed provinces, became central to that decision.

title: The Indian Independence Act is passed
detail: The Indian Independence Act created the legal basis for the new states of India and Pakistan. With it, the partition of Bengal became certain.

title: Independence, but uncertainty remains
detail: Pakistan and India became independent on August 14 and 15, but the exact border was still unclear. People in Bengal entered independence amid deep uncertainty.

title: The Radcliffe Line divides Bengal
detail: The publication of the Radcliffe Award divided Bengal into West Bengal in India and East Bengal in Pakistan. Long-standing social, economic, and geographic connections were abruptly broken.

title: Mass displacement and population reshaping
detail: Partition drove the movement of millions of people. Large-scale displacement of Hindu and Muslim communities transformed Bengal's social structure for decades to come.

title: The beginning of linguistic and cultural conflict
detail: Resistance grew in East Bengal against the attempt to impose Urdu as the sole state language. That tension would later culminate in the Language Movement of 1952.

title: From identity crisis to the road to independence
detail: The partition of 1947 created political, economic, and cultural inequalities in East Bengal. Over time, those inequalities contributed to the path that led to the independence of Bangladesh in 1971.
